title: Cellular Networks & Mobile Data
summary: The high-level architecture of cellular data networks, handoffs, and generations an interviewer expects for mobile-context questions.

slides.markdown:
**Cellular networks** cover an area by dividing it into **cells**, each served by a tower (base station); your phone hands off from one cell to the next as you move, ideally without you noticing.

- Coverage comes from many small, overlapping cells, not one giant tower.
- The network — not you — decides which tower serves you, and quietly reassigns you as you move.
- Each "G" (3G, 4G, 5G) is a real architectural shift, not just a marketing speed bump.

![A geographic area divided into hexagonal cells, each served by its own tower](assets/cellular-cell-layout.svg)

Cells overlap at their edges by design — a phone needs to be in range of the *next* tower before it can hand off from the current one, or the call/session would drop mid-transition.

assets.alt: A geographic area divided into hexagonal cells, each served by its own tower

slides.markdown:
- **3G** — first generation with real mobile data; slow by today's standards (hundreds of kbps to a few Mbps).
- **4G/LTE** — all-IP network (voice became data via VoLTE), much higher throughput (tens to hundreds of Mbps), the generation that made mobile video and modern apps usable.
- **5G** — not just "faster 4G": new radio spectrum, and architecture built for massive device density and low latency, not just phones.

Each jump changed what class of application was realistically usable over cellular.

Handing off between towers mid-session — a call, a download — has to happen without the connection resetting. The cellular network handles **mobility management** at its own layer: your device is handed to a new tower with minimal interruption, ideally invisible above the radio layer.

But the *application's* connection on top can still see the effect: TCP identifies a connection by IP/port, and a handoff sometimes changes your IP, breaking it outright. This is a big part of the motivation for QUIC's **connection migration** — see [quic-http3](quic-http3) — which survives an IP change that would kill a plain TCP connection.

5G is usually described around three distinct pillars, each targeting a different use case:

- **eMBB** — consumer-facing: much higher peak throughput for streaming, downloads.
- **mMTC** — supporting an enormous density of low-power devices per cell (IoT sensors, smart meters) 4G wasn't designed to handle at that scale.
- **URLLC** — sub-10ms latency with very high reliability, for industrial automation or remote-controlled equipment.

Most consumers only experience the first pillar — the other two are why 5G matters for IoT and industrial use, not just "phones load faster."

![A phone mid-call moving from Tower A's coverage into Tower B's, handing off before A's signal drops](assets/cellular-handoff.svg)

The network monitors signal strength from neighboring towers continuously and initiates the handoff *before* the current tower's signal becomes unusable — a well-executed handoff is imperceptible; a poorly-timed one is the dropped call everyone's experienced.

assets.alt: A phone mid-call moving from Tower A's coverage into Tower B's, handing off before A's signal drops

slides.markdown:
| | Wi-Fi | Cellular |
|---|---|---|
| Controls the network | You (or your ISP/router owner) | The carrier |
| Typical latency | Lower (short hop to internet) | Higher (more infrastructure hops) |
| Cost model | Flat | Often metered by data usage |
| Mobility | Limited to AP range | Seamless handoff across a coverage area |

**How to decide:** rarely a real choice for the user — devices prefer Wi-Fi when available and fall back to cellular for mobility. For engineers: assume cellular clients have higher, more variable latency.

slides.subTitle: Cellular isn't a wired link
slides.markdown: A mistake engineers make testing only on wired or Wi-Fi connections: **assuming cellular loss and jitter behave like a stable wired link.** Cellular links have inherently higher and more *variable* latency (radio conditions change as a user moves, towers hand off, signal degrades near cell edges) and higher packet loss under poor conditions. An app tuned only against a stable office Wi-Fi connection — aggressive timeouts, assuming steady latency for real-time features — will misbehave badly for cellular users, timing out or stuttering on connections that are simply *behaving normally* for that medium, not actually broken.
